definition: Roving is an intermediate fiber strand, finer than sliver and held together by a small protective twist or by rubbing, that feeds the ring spinning frame.
explanation: In the cotton ring-spinning route, drawn sliver is too thick to go straight to the spinning frame, so a roving frame (also called simplex, speed frame or flyer frame) draws it down further. The machine performs three tasks: drafting between rollers, inserting a low twist with a rotating flyer, and winding the strand onto a bobbin. That twist is only enough to let the fragile strand survive winding, unwinding and creel handling, since the ring frame's drafting rollers must still be able to draw it out.
example: A trainee in a cotton mill sees large bobbins of soft, thick strand hanging in the ring frame creel. Pulled gently, the strand drifts apart rather than snapping, because it carries only a few dozen turns per meter. That weakness is intentional: the drafting rollers of the ring frame need the fibers to slide past one another before the final twist is inserted.
caution: Roving is not yarn and is not meant to go into fabric. The word is used more loosely elsewhere: hand spinners may call a thick, untwisted fiber preparation roving, and in composites glass-fiber roving is a bundle of continuous filaments. Rotor spinning feeds drawn sliver directly, so a rotor-spun yarn has no roving stage at all.
deeper: Typical cotton roving frames apply a draft of roughly 6 to 15, insert about 30 to 65 turns per meter, and run flyers at around 700 to 1,300 rpm. Because the bobbin grows as it fills, the winding speed must be adjusted continuously so that roving tension stays constant as package diameter increases; older frames did this with mechanical differential gearing and newer ones with separately controlled drives. Twist is a compromise: too little lets the roving stretch and break in the creel, while too much makes it resist drafting at the ring frame. For this reason the roving stage is often described as a necessary but costly step in ring spinning.
origins: The word roving has long been used in English for a lightly twisted strand prepared for spinning, and the flyer that twists it is a descendant of the flyer on the treadle spinning wheel. Cotton mills once used a sequence of slubbing, intermediate and roving frames to reach the right fineness; modern practice usually condenses this into a single simplex step between the drawframe and the ring frame.

definition: A mechanical compressive-shrinkage finish, associated with the Sanforized trademark, that preshrinks woven cotton fabric lengthwise so the finished cloth shrinks little in later washing.
explanation: Weaving and wet processing stretch cotton fabric lengthwise, and washing lets the yarns relax, so untreated cloth shrinks. Sanforizing forces that shrinkage to happen in the mill. The fabric is dampened and heated, then carried on a thick, elastic rubber belt that is stretched as it wraps around a roller and then contracts; the fabric pressed against the belt surface is compacted lengthwise along with it. A heated drying cylinder then sets the compacted structure. The target is a low residual shrinkage specified by the trademark owner's standard.
example: Two lots of the same denim are sewn into jeans, one sanforized and one left unsanforized, as some raw denim is. After a hot wash, the unsanforized pair shortens noticeably in the leg while the sanforized pair stays close to its labeled length. A student can measure marked squares before and after washing to calculate percent shrinkage in each direction.
caution: Sanforized is a trademark for a certified process result, not a generic synonym for any preshrinking. It mainly controls lengthwise relaxation shrinkage in woven fabrics; it does not prevent shrinkage from felting, heat damage or poor garment construction. Unsanforized fabric is not defective; some buyers choose it deliberately so the garment shapes itself to the wearer through washing.
deeper: Residual shrinkage is measured by marking benchmarks on a specimen, laundering and drying it under a defined procedure, and calculating percent change in each direction. Compressive shrinkage machines control the fabric's moisture content and temperature so that yarns are plastic enough to crimp more tightly; the belt's thickness and tension determine how much compaction occurs. Operators set the compaction from a prior wash test of the fabric, aiming to remove the potential shrinkage without overshrinking, which would cause later growth. Related compaction methods apply similar principles to knitted fabrics.
origins: The process was developed in the United States by Sanford L. Cluett of the shirt and collar maker Cluett, Peabody and Company, and the trademark Sanforized was coined from his first name. Mills were licensed to use the mark when their cloth met the owner's residual shrinkage standard, and the label became a familiar promise on cotton work and casual clothing in the mid-twentieth century. Denim sold as unsanforized is defined by skipping the step.

definition: Satin is a weave with long floats and widely separated, non-adjacent interlacings, giving a smooth, lustrous face dominated by either warp (satin) or weft (sateen).
explanation: In a satin, each yarn floats over several crossing yarns and interlaces only once per repeat, and neighboring interlacings are scattered rather than stepped in a diagonal. The binding points are hidden under adjacent floats, so the face looks unbroken. Light reflects specularly from the long parallel floats, which is why filament yarns such as silk or polyester in satin appear glossy. Warp-faced satins show warp floats; sateen, often cotton, is weft-faced.
example: Compare a silk charmeuse and a cotton sateen sheet. Both feel smooth and reflect light, but in the charmeuse the floats run lengthwise in the warp, while in the sateen they run crosswise in the weft. Rubbing a fingernail gently along the float direction feels slicker than across it. The long floats that give this smoothness are also why a rough ring can snag the face.
caution: Satin names a structure, not a fiber: satin can be silk, polyester, acetate or cotton. The shine comes largely from structure and filament yarns, so a lustrous fabric is not necessarily silk. Long floats trade durability for smoothness and are more prone to snagging and abrasion. Sateen and satin are related but face in different directions.
deeper: A satin is defined by its repeat, the number of ends and picks before the pattern recurs, and its move or counter, the step between successive interlacings. The smallest regular satin has a five-end repeat; eight-end satins are common and are sometimes written 8/3 to show the move. A regular satin needs a move greater than one, less than the repeat minus one, and sharing no common factor with the repeat, so that interlacings never touch. With only one interlacing per yarn per repeat, crimp is low and yarns pack densely. Studies of weave structure report that satin fabrics differ measurably in stiffness and tensile behavior from plain and twill fabrics made from the same yarn, consistent with float length.
origins: Satin requires at least five sheds, so it demands more loom shafts or a figure-harness mechanism than plain or twill. Historically it is closely associated with silk filament, whose long smooth fibers make the most of long floats, and later with lustrous manufactured filaments and mercerized cotton sateens. This edition did not verify etymological claims about the word satin and so does not repeat them.
